interest: For historians, this file provides an extraordinarily rich, multi-layered vantage point into elite factional struggles and civil-military brinkmanship inside Tokyo during the immediate prelude to Pearl Harbor and the opening phase of World War II. It is particularly valuable for its diverse evidentiary perspectives: beyond standard State Department reporting and Ambassador Grew's candid cables, it contains confidential third-party intelligence from Vichy French diplomats, Latin American observers, Chinese military missions, corporate expatriates (such as National City Bank and Otis Elevator employees), and Korean nationalist Kilsoo K. Haan. Furthermore, the file offers unique documentation of early American wartime intelligence analysis regarding Japanese national psychology and state ideology, preserving contemporary translations of ultranationalist Shinto treatises—such as Chikao Fujisawa's Divine Mission of Nippon gathered aboard the repatriation liner M/S Gripsholm—alongside internal assessments evaluating how to counter Japanese propaganda and navigate bureaucratic rivalry among Tokyo's ruling batsu.
overview: This file documents the critical political, diplomatic, and economic developments in Japan from January 1941 through October 1942, spanning the critical months leading up to and immediately following the outbreak of the Pacific War. Compiled from U.S. diplomatic telegrams, State Department analyses, military intelligence monographs, FBI reports, and foreign observer accounts, the collection traces the internal erosion and militarization of Japanese governance. Key themes include the ideological and administrative struggles over the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (Taisei Yokusankai); the collapse of the second and third Konoye Cabinets, driven by the geopolitical shock of the German-Soviet war and the subsequent ouster of Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka; the failed unofficial peace overtures of Bishop Walsh; the ascendance of General Hideki Tojo's military administration in October 1941; the strategic debate between striking northward into Siberia versus expanding southward; acute domestic shortages, rationing, and police surveillance; and post–Pearl Harbor wartime consolidation, highlighted by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's post-repatriation reporting, the subordination of the Foreign Ministry through the creation of the Ministry of Greater East Asia, the resignation of Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo, and the propagation of State Shinto ultranationalist ideology.
